places.chef: Mitsuo Ise (井畝満夫) · founder, creator of Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki · Hiroshima, Japan · Founded in 1950 (Showa 25) as a flavor born and nurtured alongside Hiroshima's post-war reconstruction, this is the original house of Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki. places.chef: family-run anago specialist · Miyajima (Itsukushima island), Hatsukaichi, Hiroshima · A century-plus family-run institution tucked into a quiet lane within walking distance of Itsukushima Shrine. It opened in 1910 (Meiji 43) as a kappo restaurant, but the reputation of its conger eel grew so strong that around 40 years ago it pared everything back to become an anago specialist. · Restraint and respect for the ingredient. The menu is famously almost a single dish. The kitchen insists on wild-caught anago rather than farmed, favoring smaller 100-120g eels said to have the best flavor, and grills each portion over charcoal, applying the sauce only after the order is placed to keep it aromatic over the hot rice. · Anagomeshi: charcoal-grilled wild conger eel laid over a bed of Hiroshima-grown Koshihikari rice, finished with a fragrant house tare passed down through the generations.

places.chef: 井畝家 (Isoe family) · family-run okonomiyaki shop · Hiroshima City, Chuo Ward (central Hiroshima, in the Shintenchi entertainment district) · 新天地 みっちゃん carries the original 'Micchan' noren, the curtain associated with Hiroshima okonomiyaki from the very beginning. The story starts around 1950, when founder Isoe Isao (井畝井三男) set up a street stall called Mikasaya (美笠屋) on Hiroshima's Chuo-dori as the city rebuilt from the war. His son Isoe Mitsuo (井畝満夫) renamed it 'Micchan' in 1953, after his own childhood nickname. As the name spread to roughly two thousand shops across the prefecture, this Shintenchi shop kept the founder's legitimate line: the original noren was passed directly within the family to the second daughter. · Preserving the postwar Showa-era recipe and griddle technique that began with the founder's street stall, including the long-standing 'Okonomiyaki Special.' · Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki layered on a thin wheat crepe with cabbage, pork, egg and noodles, finished on the iron griddle with a house sauce refined over decades.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki is built on a wheat-flour crepe layer and steamed wheat noodles (soba/udon), and the finishing sauce is wheat-based. There is no documented gluten-free option or dedicated preparation here.

places.chef: Family-run oyster specialty shop, multi-generational · Miyajima (Hatsukaichi, Hiroshima) · Founded in 1948 on Miyajima, Yakigaki no Hayashi is widely regarded as the birthplace of grilled oysters in Japan, said to be the first shop to serve cooked grilled oysters to customers. The founder's grandfather, who ran what was then Hayashi Shokudo (Hayashi Food Hall), wanted to do something no one else was doing and began offering grilled oysters year-round, and the shop was also an early pioneer in serving raw oysters at a time when raw oysters were not popular in Japan. It sits in roughly the middle of the Omotesando shopping street, about an eight-minute walk from Miyajima port. · The family aims to preserve the original taste of the birthplace shop, grilling oysters fresh after each order using techniques handed down since founding, and serving only premium oysters. · Charcoal/steam-grilled oysters cooked fresh to order, plus year-round raw oysters and oyster rice (kaki-meshi)

places.chef: okonomiyaki teppan kitchen · A Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki house standing a minute's walk from the Peace Memorial Park, where the griddles run all day in a room built around the look of a mid-Showa (1950s-60s) building. The signature Nagataya-yaki, generous with green onion and egg and filled with shrimp and squid, is the house favorite.

places.chef: specialist noodle shop · Hiroshima · This is a counter-style specialist devoted to Hiroshima tsukemen — chilled wheat noodles served with a fiery, addictive dipping sauce, piled with fresh vegetables and pork. The house traces its lineage directly to Shin Kaen, the shop credited as the birthplace of Hiroshima cold noodles. The flagship Tokaichi shop opened in 1985, and at a time when the dish was treated as a seasonal item served only from spring through autumn, this house became the first specialist to offer it year-round. places.chef: 中村洋子 (Yoko Nakamura) · owner, proprietress, barista · Hiroshima, Japan · 中村屋 opened in 1946, the year after the atomic bomb, when the founder — a war veteran who survived the blast — first built a barrack shop in the ruined city and later moved to its current location in Sakaimachi. He recreated the Western, church-like architecture from his memories of buildings he had seen during his military service. For decades it was a fixture of Hiroshima's Showa coffee-house culture and a pioneering 'music cafe,' once hosting live jazz; jazz records still play in the background today. · A faithfully preserved Showa-era refuge — arched ceilings, a chapel-like room, chandelier lighting and antique coffee mills displayed like icons — kept running quietly out of devotion to the place and its regulars rather than expansion. · Self-roasted coffee served nel-drip style, plus simple kissaten classics like butter toast (grilled on both sides) and a long-running morning set.

places.chef: family-run, hand-made soba shop, proprietress-run (okami keeps a shop blog) · The soba tradition originates in the Izumo region of Shimane Prefecture; the family brought that recipe and technique to Hiroshima. · A family-run hand-made soba shop dating back over a century (founded 1919), carrying on the Izumo soba style passed down from the current proprietor's grandfather, now served in central Hiroshima just west of the Peace Memorial Park, near the Kannon-machi streetcar stop on the Hiroden main line. · Hand-made soba, made fresh and visible to guests at an open soba-making station at the counter. · Izumo-style soba made with whole buckwheat grains including the dark husk, giving an aromatic, robust noodle. Served in the classic Izumo styles - warigo soba (stacked round lacquer tiers over which you pour the sauce tier by tier) and kamaage soba (hot soba served in its cooking water) - alongside three-variety (san-mi) soba sets served with egg, grated yam, and grated daikon.

places.chef: okonomiyaki shop, Okonomimura red-noren '八昌' (name dates to 1965) · Hiroshima; the 八昌 name in Okonomimura dates to 1965 · The red-noren '八昌' traces back to 1965, when Furuta Takanori (古田隆則) - the eldest son of Furuta Shozaburo (古田正三郎), the first head of Okonomimura - opened it on the ground floor of the then prefab-era Okonomimura building. places.chef: family-run okonomiyaki house, post-war origin shop of Hiroshima okonomiyaki · Hiroshima, Naka Ward (Shintenchi) · One of the original Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki houses, with roots going back to a street stall that began operating along the Nagare River in 1947, in the years just after the war. In 1954 a woman named Kawara Shizuko took over the stall, and the business grew from a post-war yatai into the long-standing teppan house it is today. It has remained family-run and is often cited as one of the genuine 'origin' shops of Hiroshima okonomiyaki. · The shop describes itself as something created in Hiroshima just after the war and prides itself on staying unchanged over time, delivering the same value to its customers for more than half a century. · Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki cooked on a large L-shaped griddle, with layered wheat batter, cabbage, noodles and the shop's own sweet-and-spicy sauce.

places.n: ロペズ (Lopez)
places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Born and raised in Guatemala during its civil war, he left the country after graduating high school. Under an uncle in New Orleans, USA, he trained at Italian and French restaurants, acquiring the fundamentals of cooking such as knife work and handling meat. During temporary work at a luxury hotel in Honolulu he met and married Makiko, a native of Hiroshima, and moved to Hiroshima in 1995. He then trained at the long-established Hiroshima okonomiyaki restaurant "Hassho" before going independent, opening his own place near JR Yokogawa Station in 2000.

places.chef: kaiseki restaurant, private-room dining house · Central Hiroshima, Nakaku Mikawa-cho · A long-established Japanese kaiseki house in the heart of Hiroshima, tucked into a side street off the bustling central shopping arcade between Hondori and Hacchobori, a short walk from Peace Memorial Park. Founded in 1963, it has been welcoming guests for well over half a century, and is set across several floors with counter seating, sunken-hearth tatami rooms, and private rooms sized from intimate pairs to large parties. · Rather than avant-garde experimentation, the kitchen honors traditional preparation to draw the maximum flavor from premium ingredients, pairing dishes with house-made condiments and serving each at its optimal moment. The house emphasizes omotenashi — attentive, refined hospitality in a calm adult atmosphere. · Seasonal Seto Inland Sea seafood — fugu (pufferfish) courses with house-made plum paste and ponzu, year-round oyster courses popular with out-of-prefecture visitors, anago (conger eel), and sashimi — alongside mountain ingredients from the Chugoku region. The kitchen makes its own soy sauce and ponzu.

places.chef: independent local coffee shop · Hiroshima, Japan · Opened in 1946 in the immediate aftermath of the war, this Otemachi coffee house sits along the Takanosashi shopping arcade, a short walk south of the Peace Memorial Park. places.chef: 曽利 修 (Sori Osamu) · owner, chef · Hiroshima, Japan · Owner Sori Osamu was born in Hiroshima in 1974 and grew up eating the city's signature Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki. He spent years running a yakiniku and teppanyaki restaurant before stepping away into another industry, and once his children had grown more independent his desire to cook for people returned. He opened Soriya in December 2018, bringing roughly 18 years of professional griddle experience. · He named the place 'そり家' using the character 家 (home) rather than 屋 (shop) so guests would feel they were coming to someone's home. places.chef: owner-operator / founder · Hiroshima (founded here in central Funairi, Naka Ward) · Kisaku opened in central Hiroshima in 2001 as an ordinary ramen shop, but the owner struggled to draw customers. Determined to turn things around, he traveled to Sichuan Province in China to study tantanmen at the source, then spent time experimenting back home to adapt what he had learned. The result was a soup-less tantanmen that went on to become a Hiroshima staple, with Kisaku widely regarded as the original shop that started the city's now-famous shirunashi tantanmen. · A generous, no-frills counter ethos: a single dish done well, adjustable spice levels (including half and quarter heat), and famously cheap white rice (about 50 yen) offered all-you-can-eat to pair with the noodles. · Soup-less tantanmen kept deliberately minimal: just noodles, green onion and ground meat, dressed in a secret sauce that marries chicken and dried-sardine broth with the tingling numbness of Sichuan peppercorn (sansho/huajiao). Diners are told to lift and toss the noodles from the bottom at least ten times before eating so the sauce coats everything.
places.gfd: The single signature dish is soup-less tantanmen built on wheat ramen noodles, so it is not gluten-free. The kitchen builds satisfying, meat-style dishes entirely from plants, leaning on wheat gluten, soy protein, and okara-konjac to recreate hearty textures. · The group's guiding idea is that the foundation of all of life is what we eat — '生活すべての基本は食生活から' — and that the most delicious food is also 'kind and joyful to both body and mind' (からだにも心にもやさしく、うれしい). As a university student he and three friends launched a venture pulling rickshaws on Miyajima, which led him to study the island's history and culture to answer tourists' questions, before turning toward the world of coffee. In 2006 he opened his first self-roasted-coffee cafe at age 23, keeping it open until midnight in a back-alley spot with few customers. places.chef: Toshiaki Fujimoto · owner, chef · Hiroshima · A family ramen shop with roots going back more than 60 years. The lineage began with the grandfather, who started a noodle-making business after returning from Manchuria; that led the father to open the original shop, named simply 上海 (Shanhai), in the Nobori-cho area of central Hiroshima. The business later moved to its current Hatchobori location and became 上海総本店. It has been run by the Fujimoto family across generations, with the third generation now running operations and younger family members working in the shop. · Preserving an unbroken flavor across generations. The soy-based tare has been continuously topped up since the shop opened, keeping the taste alive over the decades. · Old-style Hiroshima chuka-soba (ramen): a rich pork-bone and soy-sauce broth (simmered roughly 6 hours) with medium-thick straight noodles, served with generous toppings of bean sprouts, green onion and menma; the wonton ramen and char siu are longtime favorites.

It grew from its main shop into around six branches across Hiroshima and Tokyo (the Tokyo location has been featured in the Michelin Guide), but the original honten remains the heart of the operation. · The kitchen aims for a savory but not heavy okonomiyaki, leaning on crisped noodles and aromatic ginger and garlic rather than weight, which has earned a loyal local following. · Its signature dish is the original 国泰寺焼き (Kokutaiji-yaki): instead of the usual pork belly it uses tontoro (pork jowl), cracks a whole egg into the center, dusts the batter with bonito powder, crisps the thin noodles by drizzling oil around the edges, and finishes with ginger and garlic for a flavor described as rich yet refreshingly light.

places.chef: izakaya, oyster specialist, grill · Hiroshima, Japan · An izakaya in Hiroshima's Yagenbori nightlife quarter built around two pillars: 100% Hiroshima-grown oysters and a theatrical cooking style called suishou-yaki, or crystal grilling. The owners source oysters directly from local producers rather than through wholesale markets, aiming for daily premium freshness, with raw oysters offered into spring and grilled oyster preparations served year-round. · A focus on local Hiroshima ingredients sourced as freshly and directly as possible, presented through showy tableside cooking. · Suishou-yaki crystal grilling, where meat and vegetables are cooked on a crystal-stone plate said to use far-infrared heat to keep the meat juicy, finished tableside with a dramatic flambe to seal in the umami. Signature ingredients include Sera Minori beef and local pork, alongside Hiroshima oysters and conger eel.

places.chef: Mamoru Nakasako (中迫守) · founder, okonomiyaki/teppanyaki chef · Yayoi-cho, central Hiroshima · A Hiroshima okonomiyaki and teppanyaki institution founded in 1970 by Mamoru Nakasako. The shop's familiar name, 'Naka-chan,' comes from the founder's own affectionate nickname. Decades on, it remains a small, bustling counter-and-table spot beloved by locals and visitors alike, filling up the moment its doors open. · Keep serving the same beloved, generously prepared Hiroshima comfort food that has drawn regulars for half a century, cooking until the day's ingredients run out. · The house signature is 'uni-cresson' (sea urchin and watercress on the teppan with butter, soy sauce and lemon) — a dish the original owner invented after drawing inspiration from Western cooking, and one credited here as its birthplace. Alongside it are classic Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki, a wide spread of teppanyaki and izakaya plates (dozens of menu items in all), and prized local oyster dishes in winter.

places.chef: owner-operated, oyster bar · Miyajima island, Hiroshima · tuGiico opened on October 1, 2021, in a renovated traditional wooden townhouse tucked along an alley between Miyajima's machiya street and the Omotesando shopping arcade, a short walk from Itsukushima Shrine. places.chef: owner, soba chef · Hiroshima (Noboricho, Naka-ku) · A small, owner-run handmade soba shop tucked into the Noboricho district of central Hiroshima, a short walk from the downtown tram stops. The family's connection to traditional food runs deep — the owner's roots trace back to a Meiji-era dengaku (skewered tofu) teahouse run by his father. The owner came to soba through his brother, who was devoted to the craft, and the two worked side by side refining their own noodle. · The shop uses only carefully selected buckwheat and adds no binding flour, letting the grain itself carry the aroma, texture, and the satisfying slip down the throat that defines great soba. · Juwari soba — 100% buckwheat noodles cut with no wheat binder. The house is known for a signature 'shogen' (笙幻) soba: an unusually pale, almost translucent, glossy noodle prized for its smooth texture and clean finish, offered alongside other styles such as sarashina and inaka (rustic).
places.gfd: The house specialty is kiko juwari soba — 100% buckwheat noodles made with no wheat binder (tsunagi), so the noodles themselves are naturally wheat-free. However, this is a traditional soba shop with no documented gluten-free program: the dipping broth (tsuyu) is made with standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat, and tempura is wheat-battered. There is also no information confirming a dedicated buckwheat-only kitchen, so cross-contact with wheat is likely. A celiac or highly sensitive…
places.vgd: Soba broth (tsuyu) is traditionally made with bonito/fish dashi, so standard cold and hot soba here should be assumed non-vegan. No vegan menu or vegan dashi is documented, so a vegan diner…

places.chef: owner-chef, stone-mills his own buckwheat in-house, certified sake sommelier (唎き酒師) who curates the sake list · Hiroshima (Danbara district, Minami Ward) · A small, owner-run soba specialist tucked into the Danbara neighborhood east of Hiroshima Station, honored with a Bib Gourmand in the 2018 Michelin Guide Hiroshima. It has built a quiet reputation among soba lovers as an 'adults' hideaway' (大人の隠れ家的お店) rather than a flashy destination. · A commitment to handmade soba crafted from flour the owner stone-grinds himself, beginning with carefully sourced whole buckwheat. Milling everything in-house is described as uncommon among Hiroshima soba shops. · Handmade soba made from buckwheat the owner stone-grinds in-house. He starts from whole, unhulled buckwheat kernels (玄蕎麦), removes the shells and impurities, then mills the flour himself with a stone mill before cutting each batch by hand. Signature dishes are cold seiro soba and a prized anago (conger eel) tempura; duck nanban and side dishes like dashimaki tamago and agedashi tofu round out the menu.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. Soy sauce-based tsuyu is used throughout. No vegan menu or documented plant-based accommodation.

places.chef: 寺西隆幸 (Takayuki Teranishi) · owner, roaster, barista · Hiroshima · Teranishi Coffee was opened in 1978 by Takayuki Teranishi after he spent about two years training at the renowned Nishimura Coffee in Kobe, where he learned to brew and absorbed a deep commitment to craft. places.chef: oyster farmer, restaurateur · Hiroshima, Japan · Kanawa traces its roots to 1867 (Keio 3), when Hisataro Miho began oyster farming as a family enterprise in Hiroshima. By the postwar years the third generation opened fresh raw-oyster counters in Tokyo and Osaka department stores (from 1946), introducing Hiroshima oysters to the capital for the first time. In 1963 the family opened this floating restaurant, reviving the Edo-period tradition of the 'kakibune' (oyster boat) that had once been used to sell and serve oysters along the rivers. · The house prioritizes safety and quality by sourcing oysters from the clean, high-salinity offshore waters of Dakokujima (Fukaura) rather than the inner bay. Moored opposite Peace Memorial Park, it also frames the act of sharing Hiroshima oysters as a small contribution to lasting peace. · Hiroshima oysters served raw, grilled, fried, and as oyster rice, alongside Seto Inland Sea seafood, eaten aboard a traditional moored oyster boat on the Motoyasu River.
places.gfd: This is a traditional oyster and seafood restaurant with no documented gluten-free program. There is no published information about gluten-free menus, dedicated fryers, or cross-contamination controls. A celiac or gluten-sensitive diner should not assume any dish is safe without a careful direct conversation, a…

Sauces use fish-based dashi and soy sauce. There is no documented vegan or vegetarian menu, and the concept is fundamentally seafood-centric, so it is not a suitable destination for vegan or vegetarian diners.

places.chef: shellfish izakaya, seafood specialist · A small specialist shellfish izakaya in Hiroshima's Yagenbori nightlife quarter, devoted to kai (shellfish) from across Japan. The team travels directly to markets from Hokkaido in the north to Kyushu in the south, building relationships with trusted suppliers to bring in carefully chosen shellfish daily. · Showcase seasonal shellfish at their peak with minimal preparation, offering each variety raw, grilled, or simmered so guests can taste its natural aroma and umami; staff suggest pairings such as oysters with white wine and raw shellfish with sake. · Shellfish in every form: shellfish sashimi (a signature), grilled oysters, oyster kamameshi (clay-pot rice), and a shellfish-dashi chawanmushi. places.chef: owner · Hiroshima · A Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki shop tucked into a counter spot in the station-front food hall, built around an unusually all-in-house approach. The team runs its own dedicated okonomiyaki-noodle factory, pressing fresh noodles for a chewy, springy bite you do not get from bought-in noodles. · The cooks describe themselves as iron-plate craftsmen who use no chemical seasonings at all, aiming to let the natural flavor of the ingredients carry the dish. To that end they make their own 'crystal' sauce, blending Seto Inland oysters and Hiroshima lemon to pair with okonomiyaki rather than relying on a generic sweet sauce; the lighter, less-sweet sauce is what makes the grated-daikon topping work so well. · Their signature okonomiyaki is finished with a free mound of grated daikon on top, which lightens the whole thing and plays against the sauce. Beyond the standard pork-and-noodle build, the kitchen leans into Hiroshima and Seto Inland specialties: oyster butter-yaki, rare beef shoulder (koune), miso-cooked beef lung, white-grilled conger eel, fried fish-cake (gansu), and a slow offal stew of several cuts in an original broth.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The dish is Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki built on a thin wheat-flour batter and layered with house-made wheat (Chinese-style) noodles. The house "crystal" sauce and standard toppings also make this unsuitable for those avoiding gluten. No gluten-free menu or accommodation is documented.

places.chef: family-run sweets shop, momiji manju maker · Miyajima, Hiroshima · Founded in 1933, Kimuraya Honten is a family-run momiji manju shop standing on a prominent corner right where the Omotesando shopping street begins on the approach to Itsukushima Shrine. For generations it has made its maple-leaf cakes by hand, and visitors can watch the manju being baked right at the storefront. · The shop deliberately keeps its original formulation and traditional dough, making its momiji manju without emulsifiers or additives — reportedly one of the only makers on Miyajima to do so, which appeals to families and additive-conscious visitors. · Momiji manju with a notably firm, chewy dough that sets it apart from the softer versions sold elsewhere on the island, filled with a sweet, sticky adzuki bean paste made to the original recipe. Beyond the classic red-bean version, the shop offers fillings such as soy-milk cream, cheese, raisin, pumpkin, and chestnut.

It is run as a small team built around the owner. · A minimal, ingredient-forward approach described as okonomiyaki 'made with the eater in mind' rather than relying on heavy technique. · Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki cooked with a distinctive light touch: a slightly thick batter is laid down and topped with plenty of fish powder, cabbage, salt and pepper, tenkasu, rinsed bean sprouts, and two slices of pork belly. The cook uses no binding agents, spreads lard onto the griddle rather than over the food, and does not press the okonomiyaki down with the spatula, instead letting high heat steam it so it stays voluminous and never squeezed dry. The fresh noodles (from Isono Seimen) are seasoned right on the griddle with dashi, salt, and garlic powder rather than being pre-sauced.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki here is built on a wheat-flour batter, topped with wheat noodles (fresh ramen from Iso Seimen), tenkasu (fried wheat batter bits), and finished with wheat-containing okonomiyaki/Carp-brand sauce. There is no indication of any gluten-free preparation, and the single shared teppan means heavy cross-contact with wheat.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The okonomiyaki is made with generous fish powder (魚粉), pork belly, and egg, and the noodles are seasoned with dashi on the griddle; the sauce is standard (non-vegan) okonomiyaki sauce. The menu centers on pork-and-egg-and-noodle okonomiyaki, with no documented vegan option.

places.chef: Kono Noriaki · third-generation owner, night-shift cook · Hiroshima · The shop began in 1945 as a nameless stall a couple opened in the black market in front of Hiroshima Station right after the atomic bombing. After an eviction it moved to the Nagarekawa entertainment district, and after a fire it settled at its current location, where it has now run for about 41 years. Third-generation owner Kono Noriaki (河野憲昭) worked as a banker until 55, then took early retirement to carry on the family business, standing at the counter twelve hours a day except Sundays. · Old-fashioned home cooking with simple seasoning that never tires the palate, so regulars keep returning; about forty pre-made side dishes are served instantly, a style born from early customers who were rushed taxi drivers and nightlife workers. · Kare-jiru (curry soup): a light, soothing thinned curry simmered with potato, onion, carrot, beef and beef tendon, finished with a house dashi of kombu, sardine and bonito.

places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The curry soup contains beef and beef tendon and a fish-based dashi (kombu, iriko, katsuo); side dishes include meat, fish roe and egg. No plant-based options documented.

places.chef: JA Zennoh (operator) · Opened March 29, 2018 at the ekie commercial complex inside JR Hiroshima Station, on the first floor. · The restaurant is part of the みのりみのるプロジェクト (Minori Minoru Project), launched in 2010 by JA Zennoh, the national federation of Japan's agricultural cooperatives, with its first shops opening that September at Ginza Mitsukoshi in Tokyo. The Hiroshima ekie location is the seventh in the series. The project was created so that producers and consumers could connect through food and farming, showcasing domestic, seasonal regional produce. · Built on the idea of 'producers and consumers thinking of one another through food and agriculture,' emphasizing local-production-for-local-consumption (地産地消) and regional revitalization, here highlighting Hiroshima and the broader Chugoku and Shikoku regions. · Teishoku set meals built around local ingredients — the signature みのる定食 lets diners choose two mains from a rotating lineup, served with rice and miso soup. Standout dishes include a Hiroshima wagyu-and-pork hamburg developed with JA Zennoh Meat Foods and steak/rice bowls featuring Hiroshima wagyu branded 'Motonari'.

places.chef: cafe, restaurant, gelateria · An open-air riverside Italian cafe that opened on August 1, 2008, on the green riverbank at the eastern end of the Motoyasu Bridge, directly across the water from Hiroshima's Peace Memorial Park and within sight of the Atomic Bomb Dome. places.gfd: No gluten-free offering is documented. The menu centers on wood-fired pizza, fresh pasta, and bread, all wheat-based, so this is not a suitable destination for someone requiring gluten-free dining. No celiac-safe preparation or dedicated handling is mentioned anywhere.

places.chef: Hirano (平野満代) · owner, chef · Hiroshima · A neighborhood okonomiyaki shop in the Minamimachi (皆実町) district that opened in 1989 and has been run, for more than three decades, by its founder Hirano-san, who cooks alone behind the counter. Warm and talkative, she has become as much of a draw as the food, and the shop has the easy, lived-in feel of a true local institution. · Her stated outlook is simple: as long as customers enjoy eating it, that's enough for her. She cooks without added oil, relying on the rendered fat from quality Hiroshima (Sera) pork, and uses firm noodles chosen to keep the dish from turning soggy, aiming for something filling yet light. · The house signature is 'soba rice' (そばライス): a hearty okonomiyaki layered with plenty of cabbage, pork, egg and yakisoba noodles, with sauce-coated rice folded in. It was born in the early years when a hungry high-school boy told her the standard size 'won't fill me up,' prompting her to build a more filling version that became the shop's defining dish.

places.chef: family-run, three-generation, broth still prepared by previous-generation owner · Hiroshima, started as a street-stall (yatai) ramen operation · A family-run Hiroshima ramen shop that has been serving the same pork-bone, soy-sauce-based chuka soba for around 40 years. places.chef: 児玉 (Kodama) · owner, chef · Hiroshima (central Naka-ku) · Founded in 1924 (Taisho 13), Gonbei is regarded as Hiroshima's oldest oden house. It began as a kaiseki restaurant where oden was first served almost as an appetizer while diners waited for their main courses, gradually becoming the dish the place is now known for. Originally in the western entertainment quarter before the war, it moved after the atomic bombing and settled in the Nagarekawa/Yakenbori nightlife district in 1953. The shop is now run by Kodama, the fourth-generation proprietor. · The house links its miso oden to the older tradition of dengaku (田楽), historically served with miso: the founder chose Fuchu white miso because it most closely resembled the miso he had used during his apprenticeship in Kyoto, blending it with the house dashi to create the restaurant's distinctive sauce. · Two styles of oden: a Seto Inland Sea dashi oden and a signature white-miso oden made with Fuchu miso, including local oysters and anago (conger eel). A range of handmade items and unusual ingredients also appear, and meals are often finished with chameshi (tea rice), optionally with miso.

Not suitable for celiac travelers.

places.chef: owner-operator, okonomiyaki chef · Hiroshima, Japan · A small, family-run okonomiyaki and teppanyaki shop tucked into the Nobori-chō neighborhood in central Hiroshima, an easy walk from the Hondōri and Hatchōbori shopping streets. The proprietor honed the craft at a well-known Hiroshima okonomiyaki shop before striking out to open this independent counter spot. · The shop leans into the energy of the open counter, where guests sit close to the griddle and watch their food cooked in front of them, paired with table seats that have their own built-in teppan grills. · Hearty Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki where the noodles are spread wide and crisped on the griddle and dusted with garlic powder for a savory, energizing finish; signature plates include the house Mihera-yaki, a spicy tan-tan style okonomiyaki, and a crispy griddle-fried potato salad. There are also colour-coded topping sets (red kimchi/gochujang, black curry/cheese, white cream/cheese) and teppanyaki small plates like lotus-root butter grill and garlic shrimp.

places.chef: 吉野恭生 (Yasuo Yoshino) · owner, chef · Hiroshima · Yatsunami opened in November 2019 in the Kamihatchobori business district, a short walk from Hiroshima Castle and Shukkeien Garden (about 170m from Shukkeien-mae streetcar stop). Owner-chef Yasuo Yoshino (born 1981), who grew up in Hiroshima and discovered okonomiyaki through student part-time work, trained at well-regarded Hiroshima okonomiyaki shops and at teppanyaki restaurants in Tokyo before opening his own counter. He largely runs the place himself, cooking on the griddle in front of guests at its roughly 21 seats. · Yoshino aims to preserve the 'unchanging, old-fashioned flavors of Hiroshima' (昔ながらの変わらない広島の味) and to keep the shop a relaxed gathering place for the neighborhood. He sources locally, using Isono Seimen noodles and Otafuku sauce. · Classic Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki layered with cabbage and crisp noodles (the signature 'Yatsunami-yaki'), alongside teppanyaki such as salt-grilled corne (rare marbled beef shoulder). The slow-simmered pork-cartilage stew (豚軟骨のすじ煮込み) in a lightly sweet broth is described as the most repeat-ordered dish.
places.gfd: This is a Hiroshima okonomiyaki and teppanyaki house. Okonomiyaki is built on a wheat-flour batter/crepe and layered with wheat-based yakisoba/udon noodles (Isono Seimen), so the core dishes are not gluten-free. The house uses Otafuku okonomiyaki sauce, which is wheat-based. No gluten-free menu, preparation, or accommodation is documented, and food is cooked on a shared communal teppan griddle. Not suitable for someone requiring strict gluten-free.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The okonomiyaki batter typically contains egg and the dish is built around pork and topped with egg; signature items include pork-cartilage stew, salt-grilled beef shoulder (corne), and seasonal oysters. Sauces and toppings are animal-derived. No vegan options are documented.

places.chef: owner, late-night counter shop · 広島市中区流川町（central Hiroshima) · One of the original sources of Hiroshima-style chuka soba. The shop traces back to 1948 (Showa 23), when three ramen yatai (food stalls) appeared in postwar Hiroshima and launched the city's ramen culture; Uguisu was one of those three. The founder is said to have learned how to make soup at a small eatery in Manchuria before opening a stall in Hiroshima's Nakashinjidai district, eventually settling into the Nagarekawa shop that has watched over the neighborhood's nightlife for decades. · Old-fashioned tonkotsu-shoyu (pork-bone soy sauce) chuka soba, often ordered with a generous heap of green onions (negi chuka soba), plus simple oden simmering on the counter as a side.
places.gfd: Wheat-based ramen noodles and a soy-sauce (tonkotsu-shoyu) broth are the core of every bowl, so the signature chuka soba is not gluten-free. Oden side dishes are simmered in soy-based dashi and many oden items (fish cakes, etc.) contain wheat. This is a tiny one-person counter shop with no allergen accommodations documented. Not suitable for a gluten-free traveler.
places.vgd: The broth is a pork-bone (tonkotsu) soy-sauce base and bowls are topped with chashu pork; oden is simmered in fish/meat-based dashi. There are no documented vegan or vegetarian options. Not suitable for a vegan or vegetarian diner.

places.chef: ramen shop, izakaya, late-night eatery · Nagarekawa, central Hiroshima · A Hiroshima institution founded in 1951 (Showa 26) in the Nagarekawa entertainment district, this chuka soba shop has fed the city's nightlife for over 68 years. The current generation carries on the recipe inherited from the founder, describing it as a taste unchanged since the previous owner's day. · Preserving the founder's flavor through patient, slow cooking while making a bowl people want to eat every day. · Chuka soba in a soy-sauce-based broth simmered for more than 12 hours, paired with a secret tare aged for three weeks. The result is a deeply savory but not heavy bowl, distinct from Hakata or Onomichi styles. Unusually for a ramen shop, the menu also carries 20-plus generous side dishes, with the fried rice a standout.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The core dish is wheat ramen noodles in a soy-sauce-based broth (Japanese soy sauce contains wheat), with sides like fried rice and gyoza. No gluten-free options or accommodations are documented.
places.vgd: Not vegan. The signature broth is a soy-based pork-bone (tonkotsu) stock simmered 12+ hours, and dishes include chashu pork, pork belly, and other meat. No vegan options are documented.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] A tiny eight-seat counter gyoza shop tucked in Hiroshima's Nagarekawa entertainment district, in business for well over half a century (mid-1960s founding). It has long held a reputation as one of the city's most beloved and hardest-to-book gyoza counters.
places.chef: 千鶴子 (Chizuko) · owner, chef, proprietress (女将) · Hiroshima · A tiny eight-seat counter gyoza shop tucked in Hiroshima's Nagarekawa entertainment district, in business for over half a century (roughly 58 years, mid-1960s founding). It has long held a reputation as one of the city's most beloved and hardest-to-book gyoza counters. · She runs the whole place herself and treats it as a warm gathering spot rather than just an eatery, carefully managing the limited counter so regulars and guests are looked after. As she puts it, the gyoza skins are alive, which makes the frying difficult, so each batch demands her full attention. · Pan-fried pork gyoza, made fresh each day. The proprietress arrives around 6:30 each morning to begin her preparations, using twice-ground pork mixed with chives from Kochi and garlic from Aomori, all wrapped in specially ordered thin skins. She steam-fries dozens of gyoza at once in a lard-coated iron pan, rotating it with practiced movements.
places.gfd: Gyoza are wrapped in wheat-flour skins (thin wheat wrappers), so neither the grilled nor the fried gyoza are gluten-free. The dipping/scallion sauce is also expected to contain wheat-based soy sauce. There are no gluten-free menu items.
places.vgd: The entire menu is pork gyoza (twice-ground pork with chives and garlic) served with a scallion sauce, plus beer. There are no vegetable-only or vegan options, and the dipping sauce is not vegan-friendly.

places.chef: chef-owner, co-owner (wife) · Tokyo · The chef-owner is a Tokyo native who comes from a family with a tonkatsu background and trained at respected Tokyo cutlet houses including Butagumi in Nishi-Azabu and Takeshin in Yoyogi-Uehara before choosing Hiroshima as the place to open his own shop, which he runs together with his wife. · A craft-obsessed approach: the chef explains the provenance and feeding of each pork (for example heritage pigs raised on fermented feed), fries at low temperature to draw out the sweetness of the fat, and pays close attention to every component. · Premium breaded pork cutlets, with diners able to choose among several heritage/brand pork varieties for both loin (rosu) and fillet (hire) cuts, an unusually city-grade level of choice for a regional shop.

places.chef: Fujiwara (藤原) · owner, chef · A small, owner-run okonomiyaki and teppanyaki shop in central Hiroshima run by Fujiwara, an avowed anime and game fan who has woven those passions through the whole space. The stairwell and walls are lined with anime posters and figurines, and a maid-uniformed staff member greets guests, so the room feels as much like a hobby shop as a griddle counter. · Fujiwara puts personal, quality service and conversation ahead of volume. When tourist crowds once swelled past 100 people a day against a comfortable capacity of around 40, he chose to cap numbers rather than chase profit, so that he could keep cooking carefully and chatting with guests about anime and games. · Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki and a long list of teppanyaki dishes. Beyond the classic pork-and-noodle okonomiyaki, the shop is known for playfully named originals such as the 'Yandere-yaki,' which piles on grated mountain yam, natto, and okra for a creamy, sticky texture. The batter is built on house-made kombu-and-bonito dashi, and the cabbage is cut into large pieces for extra crunch.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] 元祖八昌 traces its roots to the red-noren 'Hassho' okonomiyaki shop and is regarded as the original of the Hassho lineage. It was opened in 1965 by the eldest son of Furuta Shozaburo, the inaugural 'village chief' who founded Okonomimura, Hiroshima's famous okonomiyaki com
places.chef: Yuka (third daughter, second-generation owner) · owner, chef · Hiroshima (Hassho lineage / Okonomimura founding family) · 元祖八昌 traces its roots to the red-noren 'Hassho' okonomiyaki shop and is regarded as the original of the Hassho lineage. It was opened in 1965 by the eldest son of Furuta Shozaburo, the inaugural 'village chief' who founded Okonomimura, Hiroshima's famous okonomiyaki complex. The shop later moved to its current Takeyacho location and took the name 元祖八昌 ('the original Hassho'). Its red storefront earned it the nicknames 'Aka-Hassho' (red Hassho), and a daruma lantern at the shop also brought the name 'Daruma Hassho.' · The owner keeps to the orthodox basics of Hiroshima okonomiyaki. The batter binder is wheat flour seasoned with egg and mirin so it deepens and supports the flavor of the ingredients rather than overpowering them, and the shop uses a slightly spicy Mitsuwa sauce as a deliberate flavor choice. · Classic Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki, notably the meat-and-egg soba okonomiyaki.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki is built on a wheat-flour batter and crepe, includes wheat noodles (soba/udon), and is finished with wheat-containing okonomiyaki sauce (Mitsuwa). No gluten-free preparation is documented.

places.chef: owner-operator · The house dish is tantsumen (担仔麺), a noodle style with roots in Taiwan, reinterpreted here in a gentle Hiroshima form. · A pocket-sized daytime noodle shop tucked on the third floor of a building in the Ginzan-cho block of central Hiroshima, a short walk from the Hatchobori shopping district. places.chef: 池田 (Ikeda) — Noboricho store manager · self-roasting coffee house, café, coffee bean retailer · Hiroshima, Japan (central Naka-ku) · A long-running Hiroshima coffee house. The Kotobukiya business began in 1947 in central Hiroshima selling coffee and beverages, formalized as a roasting wholesaler in 1951, and moved to the Noboricho location around 1952 — making this the company's flagship retail shop, in operation for over seventy years. The company sources and roasts green beans from around the world in pursuit of a mild, approachable flavor. · A welcoming specialty coffee shop that helps each visitor — even people new to coffee — discover the beans and brewing style they enjoy. Manager Ikeda believes a truly memorable cup leaves a lasting impression: he tells of a customer who carefully recreates the shop's blend at home by mixing specific proportions of beans, because the flavor stayed in their memory. · Hand-dripped coffee from roughly 30 fresh bean varieties, the location-exclusive 'Noboricho Soft Blend,' and the much-loved coffee soft-serve ice cream paired with house-made coffee jelly; also panini, buttered toast, and fruit smoothies.
places.gfd: No gluten-free offering documented. The menu centers on coffee plus wheat-based items: panini sandwiches, buttered toast, and a coffee soft-serve. No gluten-free bread or dedicated handling is mentioned anywhere on the official site or other sources.
places.vgd: Not vegan-oriented. The signature coffee soft-serve and the milk-based blend drinks contain dairy; panini and buttered toast use wheat and likely dairy. Black hand-drip coffee itself is plant-based, but no labeled vegan food options are documented.

places.chef: independent curry specialist · Founded 1985 in the Higashihiroshima area before spreading to central Hiroshima and other regions. · Keaton (also written 亀屯) began in 1985 as a curry specialty shop. It was started at the height of Japan's family-restaurant boom, founded on the conviction that to truly compete in food service you should specialize in one thing done well rather than offer a sprawling menu. From a single shop the curry grew into a well-loved name across Hiroshima Prefecture and beyond, with the Noboricho location operating as one of its branches in central Hiroshima. · A specialist's focus on curry above all else, with a recipe the shop says keeps evolving over the decades rather than standing still. · Tsuboyaki curry: a deeply spiced curry finished to order and brought to the table bubbling hot in a thick (roughly 4mm) custom-made iron pot, with the rice served separately so the curry stays piping hot throughout the meal. Diners customize toppings and dial in their heat on a playful lettered spice scale (A regular, B spicy, C extreme), with milder options for children.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. Japanese-style curry is thickened with a wheat-flour-based roux, and no gluten-free menu, dedicated preparation, or allergen accommodation is documented at this shop. Travelers with celiac disease should avoid it.
places.vgd: Not vegan-friendly. The curries are meat- and seafood-based (chicken cutlet, corned beef, special beef, seasonal fried oyster) and the wheat-flour roux is not documented as plant-based. places.chef: 島村光徳 (Mitsunori Shimamura) · owner-chef · Hiroshima Prefecture (chef born 1972 in Hiroshima) · Owner-chef Mitsunori Shimamura was born in Hiroshima in 1972 and discovered cooking through a high-school part-time job. He trained at the French campus of the Tsuji Culinary Institute, worked at leading Japanese hotels, and apprenticed in Lyon and Cannes before returning home. He was involved from the opening of Mikuni Hiroshima, then carried forward the spirit of master chef Kiyoshi Mikuni to open his own restaurant, which he renamed Shimalabo in 2017; he later opened a sister restaurant, Shimalabo Bis, in 2020. · Inheriting Mikuni's belief that 'the ingredients decide the cooking,' the kitchen builds its menus around seasonal, locally-sourced produce — especially organic, natural-farming vegetables from Watanabe Farm in Higashi-Hiroshima — and pursues sustainable, near-zero food-waste cooking. The dining room is run with a warm, home-like sense of hospitality. · Course-based 'cuisine du terroir' (la cuisine du terroir) — generous, classically-rooted French cooking that puts local Hiroshima produce and proteins at the center, with theatrical tableside service.

places.chef: operator · Hiroshima (Naka-ku) · J CAFE is a revival of a beloved Hiroshima café from the 2000s, an era when stylish cafés were proliferating across the city. places.chef: owner-operator, onigiri maker · Higashi-Hiroshima (mobile kitchen), later established on Miyajima (Itsukushima). · Santo began as a hand-made onigiri food truck based in the Higashi-Hiroshima (Saijo) area, where the owner sold carefully crafted rice balls from a mobile kitchen. places.chef: 松岡美穂子 (Miho Matsuoka) · owner, okonomiyaki cook · Hiroshima, Japan · A neighborhood okonomiyaki shop founded in 1962 (Showa 37) on Jizo-dori, a downtown shopping street in Naka-ku that locals describe as a 'shitamachi within the city.' It has operated in the same spot for over half a century and is now run by Miho Matsuoka, the third-generation owner, who says she has been cooking her own okonomiyaki here since she was in elementary school. places.chef: bakery, cafe · Hiroshima · MON is a long-established Hiroshima bakery founded in 1953 (described as a roughly 65-year-old shop). places.chef: independent tsukemen shop · Hiroshima City, Higashi-ku (Hikarimachi) · 広島つけ麺 かず is a long-established Hiroshima tsukemen specialist that began in 1997 and is credited as a 'fire-starter' (火付け役) of the Hiroshima tsukemen boom — the style itself traces back to 1954's Shinkaen. places.chef: owner · Hiroshima, central Naka-ku · A long-running independent boulangerie founded around 2004 and operated by the small local company Brio (有限会社ブリオ), this is a neighborhood institution that relocated within central Hiroshima and reopened in its current Teppo-cho spot in 2025. places.chef: owner, chef · Takehara City, Hiroshima Prefecture · The owner grew up in Takehara, a historic port town on the Seto Inland Sea, and built this small izakaya in the lively Ekinishi district just west of Hiroshima Station as a way of bringing his hometown's flavors to the city. · Rather than serving generic 'Hiroshima products,' the owner chooses the finest ingredient from the right corner of the prefecture for each dish, because flavor varies by where things are grown and raised. The sake list reflects the same homecoming spirit: only sake from three breweries in his native Takehara, including seasonal limited releases. · The house signature is negi-shabu: East Hiroshima white scallions paired with Seto Momiji pork, swished through a house-made, ginger-accented bonito dashi with a slightly sweet soy base. places.chef: Nakashio family (中塩家) · founding family bakery, third-generation owner · Kure, Hiroshima · This counter on the basement food floor of the Fukuya Hatchobori department store sells the breads of a Kure institution founded in 1936 (Showa 11). The dining room blends a calm, traditional Japanese feel with private rooms, and every seat - including the counter and the tatami rooms - has its own built-in iron griddle so food is served hot and freshly cooked right in front of you. · Built around the idea that food tastes best straight off the iron plate, the restaurant fits its private griddle into every room so groups, dates, and solo diners alike can eat freshly cooked dishes; counter guests are welcomed by an easygoing owner-chef. · Hiroshima-style okonomiyaki cooked on the teppan alongside Seto Inland Sea seafood and griddle dishes: local oysters, the Hiroshima specialty uni horen (sea urchin on sautéed spinach), salt-grilled koune (a rare, collagen-rich wagyu beef cut), and premium A5 wagyu, all paired with local Hiroshima sake.

places.chef: Souji Kimura · owner, chef · Hiroshima, Naka-ku Otemachi · A specialist devoted to anago-meshi, Hiroshima's century-old conger-eel-over-rice dish, set in Otemachi within sight of the A-Bomb Dome and Peace Memorial Park. The shop is run by owner Souji Kimura, who grew up around the trade — his father was a sushi chef — and the kitchen is led by a head chef with more than twenty years of sushi experience. · The owner inherited from his sushi-chef father the idea of preparing every dish 'with love, just as you would cook for your own children and parents,' and the shop commits to serving food as delicious as possible using premium ingredients — pairing Hiroshima's traditional anago-meshi with refined sushi technique to create a 'new Hiroshima taste.' · Three contrasting styles of anago-meshi served side by side: 'black,' raw conger grilled over charcoal for a crisp, fragrant, chewy bite; 'red,' simmered then finished with a special sweet sauce until meltingly tender; and 'white,' shirayaki grilled plain to taste the eel itself, served with real wasabi and a special soy sauce. Each set comes with soup and pickles, and the chef oversees every preparation.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The anago is served with sweet tare/soy-based sauce (the "black" and "red" styles) and the white style is served with a special soy sauce — Japanese soy sauce and sweet tare both contain wheat. No gluten-free menu, no allergen documentation, and the kitchen does not advertise any gluten-free handling. A celiac traveler could not eat safely here.
places.vgd: Not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. Every main is conger eel (fish), served over rice with miso soup and pickles, and even the white-grilled style uses soy sauce. There are no plant-based mains or documented meat/fish-free options.

places.chef: cafe, fermented-food / yogurt specialist, talk and event space · Sweden / Hiroshima · BioGaia TALKS is a fermented-food cafe and dialogue space in central Hiroshima's Kamiyacho district, near the A-Bomb Dome. It is run by the Swedish probiotics maker BioGaia, built around the idea that good gut health and good conversation nourish people together. The cafe's signature is yogurt made with L. reuteri lactic-acid bacteria, including a plain yogurt that faithfully recreates what is described as Japan's oldest yogurt recipe, born in the Nomura family of Hiroshima in 1917 and revived by the fifth generation. · The space runs on the motto that 'knowledge is the finest entertainment,' pairing a healthy, fermentation-forward menu (kin-katsu, or 'bacteria wellness') with talk events where experts and guests share ideas face to face across medicine, science, food, and art. Greenery, a nursing room, and diaper-changing facilities make it a calm, family-friendly place to eat, read, work, or attend an event. · L. reuteri yogurt and smoothies, plus body-friendly fermented lunch dishes such as amazake (sweet-sake) butter chicken curry and a neba (sticky-fermented) rice bowl, available for dine-in…

Despite a traditional Japanese-looking exterior, the kitchen is led by a chef with an Italian background who ran his own Italian restaurant for about twelve years before opening here; the owner's name is not publicly listed. · Let prized Hiroshima land-and-sea ingredients shine, cooking them simply but expertly across two culinary traditions rather than confining the food to one style. · Seasonal Setouchi (Seto Inland Sea) seafood prepared in both Japanese and Italian styles: oysters sourced directly from producers in Kure (Ondo) and Osaki served raw, grilled, or fried; white-grilled local anago with sea salt and wasabi; grilled octopus; and hearty meat dishes like a signature T-bone steak and seasonal game.
places.gfd: No gluten-free provisions are documented. places.n: Baker theta (ベイカー シータ)

places.n: Big Apple (ビッグアップル)
places.hood: 廿日市市大野 (Ōno, Hatsukaichi — Miyajima ferry-gateway area near Miyajimaguchi)
places.cu: Vegan Indian curry & cafe (falafel, tempeh, cakes)
places.notes: [GF] Fully vegan cafe a short taxi ride (~5 min) or 25-min walk from the Miyajima ferry at Miyajimaguchi — a handy plant-based stop. places.n: CoCoRoBA (米粉ぱん CoCoRoBA)
places.hood: 佐伯区利松 (Toshimatsu, Saeki-ku), Hiroshima
places.notes: [GF-dedicated] A wheat-free rice-flour bakery — the whole facility uses only domestic rice flour, so there is no wheat line to cross-contaminate. places.chef: owner, baker · Hiroshima, Japan · CoCoRoBA opened in November 2022 in Toshimatsu, Saeki-ku, Hiroshima, as a dedicated gluten-free rice-flour bread shop. It was built around the three major food allergies (wheat, egg, dairy), aiming to give allergy sufferers and health-conscious customers bread they can eat with confidence. The owner sources only domestic rice flour — a blend of Hiroshima-grown Koshihikari and Kumamoto's Mizuho Chikara variety developed for rice bread — and uses moshio sea salt from Kami-Kamagari island and sudaki unrefined cane sugar (素焚糖) from Amami Oshima, avoiding unnecessary additives. places.n: Miyajima Guest House Mikuniya (宮島ゲストハウス三國屋)
places.hood: 宮島町 (Miyajima / Itsukushima island), Hatsukaichi, Hiroshima
places.notes: [GF] One of the very few gluten-free-accommodating dining options actually ON Miyajima island, where evening/morning food is scarce. Book dinner as a guest and give advance notice for gluten-free; the base dish is a wholly plant-based original curry, so confirm the curry roux, any thickener/flour and soy sauce are wheat-free (Japanese curry roux and soy sauce normally contain wheat). places.chef: 寺澤淳也（Junya Terasawa） · owner · Miyajima (Itsukushima), Hatsukaichi, Hiroshima, Japan · 宮島ゲストハウス三國屋 is a small guesthouse on Miyajima island at 宮島町327, roughly a five-minute walk from Itsukushima Shrine. places.n: お好みハウス のんのん (Okonomi House Nonnon)
places.hood: Danbara-minami, Minami-ku (near Hijiyama Park)
places.notes: [Mom & Pop · okonomiyaki] A multi-generational, family-run okonomiyaki shop near Hijiyama Park, selected for Tabelog's "Top 100 Okonomiyaki" list multiple years running (2018, 2022-2025). Preserves a recipe passed down from a previous generation, made without added MSG. A deliberately accessibility-minded touch: the cabbage is cut finely rather than left in the long, standard sengiri strips, specifically so it is easier to eat for guests of any age. Signature is a nikutama-soba build with thin batter and finely-shredded cabbage meant to foreground the vegetables' own sweetness, finished with Otafuku sauce.
